description: UCSF Institute for Global Health Sciences IGHS Connect November theme: Climate and Health Speaker Radisti A. Praptiwi, PhD Researcher, Research Center for Ecology, National Research and Innovation Agency Radisti A. Praptiwi is a researcher in marine resources management at the Research Center for Ecology, National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) in Indonesia, where her work sits at the intersection of ecology, society, and governance. She takes an interdisciplinary approach to understanding marine and coastal systems, including how they function, what they provide, and how they can be managed to benefit both people and the planet. Her recent work focused on some of the most pressing challenges facing coastal communities: how plastic pollution disrupts coastal and marine ecosystem services and the well-being of those who rely on them, how community-based monitoring can help close critical data gaps in remote and low-resource coastal areas, and the ways climate change is reshaping cultural connections to the sea, particularly in small island settings. Moderator: Matthew Gribble, PhD Associate Chief for Research in Occupational, Environmental and Climate Medicine, UCSF

description: On November 19, Gladstone Institutes will honor the 2026 Ogawa-Yamanaka Stem Cell Prize winner, Jun Takahashi, MD, PhD. He was selected for pioneering the translation of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell biology into regenerative therapies for Parkinson’s disease, culminating in the world’s first clinical approval for iPS cell-derived cell transplantation. During this event, Takahashi will be presented with the award and give a scientific lecture based on his groundbreaking translational work. If you’re unable to attend the event in person, you can register for the livestream. About Jun Takahashi Jun Takahashi, MD, PhD, is former director and professor at the Center for iPS Cell Research and Application (CiRA), Kyoto University, Japan. He received his medical degree from Kyoto University and began his career in neurosurgery at Kyoto University Hospital. He then earned his doctorate from the Kyoto University Graduate School of Medicine and conducted postdoctoral research in the laboratory of Fred Gage at the Salk Institute, where he began his work on neural stem cells. Takahashi joined CiRA as a founding member in 2010 and was appointed professor in 2012. He then served as director of CiRA from 2022 to 2026. His research has focused on developing stem cell-based therapies for neurological disorders, particularly Parkinson’s disease. From 2018 to 2023, Takahashi’s team conducted the world’s first clinical trial of an iPS cell-derived therapy for Parkinson’s disease, work that ultimately contributed to the first regulatory approval of an iPS cell-derived therapeutic product. His honors include the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research Cell Replacement Therapy for Parkinson’s Disease Award and the Japanese Society for Regenerative Medicine Award. The Ogawa-Yamanaka Stem Cell Prize recognizes individuals whose original translational research has advanced cellular reprogramming technology for regenerative medicine. The prize was established in 2015 through a generous gift from the Betty and Hiro Ogawa Family. It also recognizes the importance of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells), discovered by Gladstone Senior Investigator and Nobel laureate Shinya Yamanaka, MD, PhD. Chosen by a committee of experts in the field, the awardee receives an unrestricted prize of $150,000 USD. The prize is supported by Gladstone and Cell Press.

description: Psychedelic Experience or Side Effect? Historicizing the Psychoactive Properties of Anesthetics in the 19th and Early 20th Centuries Jacob Green, PhD --------------------------------- In our upcoming November talk, Dr. Jacob Green will discuss how the psychedelic-like effects of nitrous oxide and ether, including hallucination-like dreams, altered thought patterns and mystical experiences shifted from being considered part of the main action of these drugs to a dangerous side effect after doctors began using them as anesthetics in the mid 19th century. This shift radically impacted doctor-patient relations. Doctors disparaged patients who reported having meaningful visions of angels and other spiritual entities under anesthesia and dismissed accounts of women who accused their providers of sexually assaulting them while they were anesthetized as anesthetically-induced hallucinations. Jacob Green, PhD, is a postdoctoral fellow at the UCSF Center for Tobacco Control, Research and Education. He received his doctorate in history from UCLA in 2025. His research interests center on the history of psychoactive drugs and their influence on culture, religion and law. At the Center for Tobacco Control Research and Education, Jacob works on documents in the Juul Labs Collection. His papers in progress address the environmental impacts of vaping, and employee health and safety issues related to vaping in the workplace. He is also working on a book project, based on his PhD dissertation, which explores how historical context shaped hallucinations and other altered states of consciousness patients experienced under anesthesia during surgeries and dental procedures in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Jacob’s work has appeared in Historical Studies in the Natural Sciences, History of Pharmacy and Pharmaceuticals and an edited volume based on the 2025 Harvard Psychedelic Intersections Conference. --------------------------------- The UCSF Drug Use Research Group (DURG) is a city-wide seminar attended by faculty, postdoctoral fellows, graduate students, and other Bay Area investigators centering on persons who use drugs. The DURG was founded in 2005 after a friendly debate between an epidemiologist and anthropologist on the merits of quantitative versus qualitative research methods. These monthly meetings provide a community platform for new and established investigators to present their works-in-progress, consult on new or related research and policy questions, and prepare for grant applications, conferences, and publications in a supportive environment. The seminar has been successful in cultivating new research collaborations, mentorship, and sustaining interdisciplinary and interprofessional dialogue between those engaged in basic sciences, epidemiology, clinical research, and qualitative methods. Our meetings are not recorded or live-streamed. If you would like to attend the seminar or present your work for dissemination, collaboration, and/or peer review, please contact Leslie Suen, MD, MAS: Leslie.Suen@ucsf.edu

description: The UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center's Office of Community Engagement presents: CAB2: Chat & Chew Lecture Series Speaker: Mark Jesus Mendoza Magbanua, MS, PhD Laboratory Medicine Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center UC San Francisco Talk Title: Can a Blood Test Help Us Stay One Step Ahead of Breast Cancer? Understanding Liquid Biopsy and Its Potential to Improve Cancer Care About the Speaker: Dr. Magbanua is a Professional Researcher/Senior Scientist in the Department of Laboratory Medicine at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). He has extensive expertise in liquid biopsy, cancer genomics, and data science, with a particular focus on advancing precision oncology in breast cancer. He leads research projects investigating circulating tumor DNA (ctNA) in the I-SPY trial, an adaptive clinical trial evaluating neoadjuvant therapies for earty-stage breast cancer. His earlier research focused on developing technologies to detect and characterize circulating tumor cells (CTs), contributing to advances in liquid biopsy research. His work has provided important insights into the clinical significance and biological characteristics of tDNA and CTCs in breast cancer. As a principal investigator of NCI-funded R01 research grants, Dr. Magbanua focuses on integrating tDNA with imaging, molecular, and clinical biomarkers to improve the prediction of treatment response and ong-term outcomes in early-stage breast cancer. His research also explores innovative approaches for solating and characterizing tumor cells and analyzing cell-free DNA in malignant effusions from patients with metastatic breast cancer. His overarching goal is to develop and clinically validate liquid biopsy technologies that enable more precise treatment decisions and ultimately improve outcomes for cancer patients. >> REGISTER TO ATTEND, powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform

description: The Academic Senate is pleased to announce the selection of Margot Kushel MD, as the recipient of the Fourth Annual Faculty Research Lectureship in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences for her groundbreaking research on homelessness, housing instability, health, and the translation of evidence into policy and systems change. The lecture, titled “Housing, Homelessness, and Health: Bringing Evidence to the Policy Discussion.” will take place on Thursday, December 10, from 3:30pm – 5:00pm at Rock Hall, 1550 4th St., on Mission Bay Campus, with a small reception to follow. The lecture will also be broadcast on Zoom. Dr. Kushel is an internationally recognized leader in health services research whose work has advanced understanding of the causes and consequences of homelessness, the relationship between housing and health, and evidence-based approaches to preventing and ending homelessness. Her work combines rigorous research with community engagement and policy translation, with particular attention to older adults and other populations experiencing structural marginalization. Over the course of her career, she has authored nearly 200 peer-reviewed publications and has served as principal investigator or co-investigator on numerous federally funded studies. A defining feature of Dr. Kushel’s work is its direct connection to policy and practice. In 2019, she established the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative (BHHI) with a $30 million gift from Marc and Lynne Benioff, bringing together researchers, people who experienced homelessness, policymakers, service providers, and community organizations to translate findings into action. She is also principal investigator of the California Statewide Study of People Experiencing Homelessness (CASPEH), the most comprehensive study of homelessness in California in decades. The study surveyed a representative sample of 3,200 adults across the state, and its findings have informed policymakers and helped reshape public understanding of homelessness and its potential solutions. Dr. Kushel has also led pioneering research on older adults experiencing homelessness through the National Institute on Aging-funded Health Outcomes of People Experiencing Homelessness in Older Middle Age (HOPE HOME) study. Since 2012, the study has generated important findings on functional decline, social isolation, health care utilization, mortality, and the “graying” of the homeless population, while informing legislation and national policy discussions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Dr. Kushel helped develop and implement responses for people experiencing homelessness, including Project Roomkey, testing and vaccination efforts, and shelter-based public health protocols. Margot Kushel, MD, is Professor of Medicine and Division Chief of the Division of Health and Society in the UCSF Department of Medicine at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital and Trauma Center. She is Director of the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative and the UCSF Action Research Center for Health. She also maintains an active internal medicine practice at the Richard Fine People’s Clinic at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital, caring for patients with complex medical and social needs. The Fourth Annual Faculty Research Lecture in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences will be held on Thursday, December 10, from 3:30pm – 5:00pm at Rock Hall, 1550 4th St., on Mission Bay Campus and will be broadcast on Zoom. The Faculty Research Lecture in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences award was established in 2023. This award is bestowed on an individual member of the UCSF faculty with outstanding achievements in social, behavioral, and health policy research. UCSF faculty are asked to consider the outstanding research contributions of their colleagues and submit nominations for this prestigious award to the Academic Senate Committee on Research. The Committee on Research selects a recipient of this award annually., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform
